title: Assessing Scotland’s sector finances
summary: The first pillar of Scotland's review of university funding looks at the current state of the sector. As DK finds, the evidence is not encouraging
full_text:
The first pillar of Scotland’s Future Framework for Universities deals with immediate, practical needs: the assessment of what Scotland needs from higher education in the future and how the current sector gets there comes later.

The message is simple and stark. For Scotland’s higher education system to keep doing what it is currently doing it needs an extra £200m, each year.

That’s the difference between TRAC expenditure and sector income in 2023-24, and it has grown steadily over the years. The deficit hits differently at different providers and for different activities – with the familiar patterns of publicly funded teaching and all kinds of research subsidised primarily by international student fees. Balancing the sustainability of a devolved sector on an income stream subject to the vagaries of increasingly inept immigration policy making at a UK government level makes the sector vulnerable.

Risk registered

That vulnerability, and the various ways in which providers need to cut spending and curtail activity to account for it, is a detriment to Scotland’s higher education sector – and therefore to Scotland as a nation. The report recognises that teaching and research are just the tip of the iceberg, noting support for industrial innovation, regional development, public services, and community wellbeing. All of these ancillary benefits are also at risk.

But the issue is not just with recurrent funding. Universities in Scotland also face a £1.1bn estates maintenance backlog, encompassing immediate priorities like the removal of potentially dangerous RAAC elements (£77.2m) and a longer term need to prepare for a future of extreme weather conditions and rising energy costs (wider commitments to net zero would cost at least £645m over the next decade).

Again, to be clear, this report is just pillar one of a much more detailed review. It does not identify underlying causes or propose policy responses. All it does is set out the current state of play, clearly and with rigour.

TRAC changes

Because we’re talking about costs of activities within higher education providers you would imagine that TRAC (Transparent Approach to Costing) data would be front and centre. It is a good dataset for doing what it does, but it has limitations (we’ve been over some of these on Wonkhe recently) and – given the level of UK-wide interest in the costs of university activity right now – you can expect to be talking about it a lot in the months to come.

Some of those limitations are very germane for this kind of study. TRAC hasn’t (since 2018-19) gotten into subject areas and cost centres. The – largely indicative – figures it generates are better in aggregate but that act of aggregation means that the huge differences in institutional circumstances are smoothed out in various ways. Instead of the usual TRAC groups we are offered “ancient universities” (St Andrews, Glasgow, Edinburgh, Aberdeen), “chartered universities” (Strathclyde, Heriot-Watt, Dundee, Stirling), “modern universities” (Glasgow Caledonian, Abertay, Napier, Queen Margaret, West of Scotland, Robert Gordon, UHI) and small specialists (Glasgow School of Art, Royal Conservatoire, SRUC).

Chartered universities (no doubt Dundee is an outlier here) have more income than expenditure, but the flattening effect of grouping financially stronger universities with weaker ones means that overall 99 per cent of this group’s projected in-year expenditure is covered by income. The report notes that TRAC’s methodology (the margin for sustainability and investment) will be flattering this figure and that in year figures are bleaker.

Teaching

In-year (HESA) data is also used to furnish six case studies that are used to illustrate issues in particular spheres of activity. In a teaching section that focuses on the decline in the amount of the cost of public teaching that public funding covers, we learn more about UWS social work provision in rural locations and the substantially higher costs that this kind of provision entails – it is a neat reminder that socially valuable provision in underserved areas is seldom cost effective.

Scotland’s ancient universities tend to be most able to access international student income, though the dwindling value of public funding for home student teaching has led other providers to attempt to increase this kind of recruitment over the past three years. While all groups have at least 40 per cent Scottish (home) students, for modern universities the proportion is nearly 80 per cent.

Research and capital

As you may well expect, Scottish universities do not recover the full cost of research via any of the common funding routes – the overall recovery rate is 72 per cent, which compares favourably with a whole UK figure of 67 per cent. Here we don’t get a breakdown by institutional type, but it is reasonable to expect that ancient and chartered universities are more likely to access the more traditional (UKRI) funding – with ancient universities (£70m) securing more overall than chartered universities (£25m) while modern providers rely more on SFC funding within a lower overall total (£1m).

In terms of maintenance and modernisation, the larger and older estates of ancient universities have seen an increase in property costs recently. As well as immediate priorities like addressing unsafe cladding and RAAC, universities will also be looking to minimise energy spending as costs are set to increase substantially – something which may also help with longer term (and potentially expensive) energy plans linked to net zero. There’s a great case study regarding Glasgow’s combined heat and power overhaul system in this section.

Uncosted activity

Running teaching and research, and maintaining estates, are some of the more expensive things that Scottish universities do. Other activity isn’t technically “uncosted” – there are of course innovation and knowledge exchange funding streams, and support of community-facing activities – but it does tend to seek subsidy to cover staffing costs in particular, and this spending is very difficult to isolate in TRAC.

The case studies here are the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland’s creative enterprise office – an uplift in SFC knowledge exchange funding enabled the launch of a free-to-access service to help develop emerging business ideas and support portfolio careers in and beyond the creative industries – and the Bright Red Triangle collaboration (Napier, Queen Margaret, Edinburgh College) designed to support student, staff, and graduate enterprise. In each case external funding was used to cover the extensive costs (which can reach up to £5m in the very largest university) of delivering knowledge exchange activities – providers highlighted the risks to such activities given tightening funding envelopes.

Student support is also difficult to cost – even when it covers government priority activity like the Student Mental Health Action Plan. The report recognises (via a Robert Gordon University case study) the growing complexity of student needs – university spending on mental health support rose by 73 per cent between 2020 and 2025, and has been supported in Scotland by time-limited funding streams.

Staff costs

While in TRAC staff costs are built into activity costs, the Pillar1a report separately analyses the impact of institutional financial pressure on pay, workload, and conditions. When even a 2 per cent (below inflation) pay increase for all staff would cost the sector £55m, it is easy to see the problem. The (new JNCHES) national bargaining scheme has led to a review of the pay spine – addressing known anomalies and compression between spine points – which could be implemented by this time next year.

Meanwhile staff (807 respondees to a UCU workload survey conducted earlier this year) report working an average 7.76 extra hours per week, with just over 61 per cent reporting an increase in workload over the last year. A decrease in staff numbers and an increase in administrative work are the most commonly cited reasons.

That administrative work links to another perennial bugbear – a legally rigorous and demanding regulatory framework. We get an overview of regulatory requirements, but commentary on the efficacy of these requirements is out of scope for this pillar 1a report.

Where this leaves us

There’s no real surprises in this report – we know that teaching and research don’t cover costs, that estates backlogs are growing, and that there is not enough money in the system to support the many other things the government would like universities to do. It is also well known that this growing financial pressure is having a detrimental effect on pay, conditions, and workload (the report does not spell out the obvious knock-on impacts for the student experience).

But with the analysis and policy recommendations still to come in later reports, the asks here are modest. The limitations of TRAC (designed and modified for more stable periods in university financial history) are becoming apparent. There is a call for the reappraisal of the need to allow TRAC costing to address individual subject areas (as used to happen in TRAC-T), and the margin for sustainability and investment (MSI) is singled out as needing an overhaul for these days of deficit: reducing required expenditure in response to falling funding makes it look like the sustainability gap is shrinking. There’s more of this in the analytical report that forms the background to this publication – I’m looking forward to diving more deeply into some of the data presented there at some point soon.

There’s also a need for better costing approaches for innovation, knowledge exchange and civic activity – and a review of the administrative reporting burden. As many of these processes are UK wide, this hints at the need for cross UK working on these issues (that affect each of the four UK HE sectors) as Wales and Northern Ireland make parallel in-depth examinations of funding models and the need for similar activity in England becomes even more apparent.

title: ‘North of the border: I think you oughta…?’: Taking a look at the Future Framework (and how Scotland has 21% more to spend on each school pupil but 24% less to spend on each undergraduate than England)

The post ‘North of the border: I think you oughta…?’: Taking a look at the Future Framework (and how Scotland has 21% more to spend on each school pupil but 24% less to spend on each undergraduate than England) appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
HEPI CEO, Nick Hillman OBE, takes a look at today’s report on Scotland’s university funding crisis.

Welcome to 2026/27

For those of us who live elsewhere, it is easy to forget that the academic year is already well underway in Scotland. For example, schools returned in mid-August and Scottish universities are now gearing up for the much earlier return of their students than occurs in, say, England.

So it makes sense that today sees the long-awaited publication from Pillar 1a of the ‘Future Framework for the Sustainability and Success of Scotland’s Universities’. Overseen by both the Scottish Government and Universities Scotland and very ably led by Professor Sir Anton Muscatelli, President of the Royal Society of Edinburgh, it is a bureaucratic mouthful for a very important project.

Building a consensus

The general idea behind the Future Framework is to find a shared consensus on the scale and makeup of Scotland’s higher education funding challenges and then, at a later stage, to work towards solutions.

This is all much more important than it might initially sound. Policymaking in Scotland is shaped by the size of its relatively small polity, meaning the political class is tighter and universities have more direct engagement with their political overlords, at least compared to England. This changes the nature of the debate, in some good ways and some bad.

Most notably, the dominance of the ruling Scottish National Party and their long-standing ‘free’ higher education policy, meaning Scottish-domiciled undergraduates who attend Scottish institutions do not have to pay tuition fees, has tended to stifle debate on alternatives. No major political party, with the possible exception of Reform UK, have promised to change tack – at least, not recently or not yet.

The Future Framework enjoys broad cross-party support and might just offer a Get-Out-of-Jail-Free card for policymakers and those running Scotland’s universities. But this is not a foregone conclusion – responding to today’s report, the Education Secretary, Màiri McAllan, yet again stressed the perceived benefits of free education:

Our joint commitment to the protection of free tuition means that Scottish students are not hampered by the levels of debt we see elsewhere in the UK, and they are able to go to university based on their ability to learn and not their ability to pay.

Funding the future

On the Future Framework’s website, today’s report is described as an ‘ambitious and evidence-based review … looking at funding of university teaching, skills development, research and innovation to ensure it is fit for the future.’ This it does admirably. The other pillars will look at ‘Future Needs to 2045’, ‘Sector-led Transformation’ and ‘Evidence-led Options for a Future Framework’.

Today’s report shows that Scotland’s higher education institutions face an overarching funding gap of £200 million a year, that the gap has existed for a while and is therefore best understood as ‘structural’ and that the gap affects the whole sector – though individual institutions (or groups of institutions) are not all affected in exactly the same way.

In short, Scotland’s institutions make money from international students, but lose even more money from a combination of shortfalls from teaching home students and conducting research. The picture is not an entirely static one: for example, in less than a decade, the proportion of total teaching income coming from international students has risen from under a third to around one-half (amounting to £1.25 billion).

The consequences

It bemuses some people that the UK higher education sector, including Scotland’s higher education institutions, complain so much yet seemingly continue to thrive – for example, in the global league tables. But as Anton Muscatelli writes persuasively in The Times today:

The consequences of financial strain are often gradual rather than dramatic. Universities do not suddenly stop functioning when budgets tighten. Instead, investment is deferred, vacancies are left unfilled, infrastructure projects are delayed and institutions look for efficiencies wherever they can. For a time, much of this can pass unnoticed from the outside, even where institutions are sounding the alarm bells. But there comes a point when pressures can no longer be managed without affecting capability. Scotland’s universities have objectively crossed that threshold.

That all seems increasingly undeniable. So if I had any criticism of today’s report, it would not be on the substance; it would focus more on the spin. I wonder if the focus should have been a little less on the headline £200 million shortfall, as I am not convinced the average voter in Scotland or elsewhere is likely to find it an especially easy figure to get their heads around. What they may want to know more is how such a sector-wide shortfall hits their children and grandchildren. The BBC have, however, helped to fill in the gap, as their calculations on the back of today’s report show ‘there was a shortage of £2,703 per Scottish student’.

It is possible to take this further by contrasting the amount spent educating Scottish school pupils with the amount spent educating Scottish undergraduates. According to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, schools have over £10,400 per pupil (21% higher than in England). In contrast, universities in Scotland receive something like £7,800 to educate each Scottish-domiciled undergraduates (24% less than the number in England, according to London Economics).

These may not be exactly comparable numbers (and I look forward to discussing the details when I am in Scotland next week), but the broad comparison certainly holds true. We used to think higher education needed more resources than schooling; we now operate as if the opposite is true, though if we have stumbled into this position more by accident than design.

Another striking comparison – one that is included in today’s report – is that Scottish students have just 82% of their true costs covered while international students pay 150% of theirs. If nothing else, this is a reminder that Scotland’s universities have done all they can to respond to their funding woes on domestic students by acting entrepreneurially in relation to other income sources.

Going it alone?

These challenges are not just a Scottish problem, however. The same sort of issues (such as losing money on home students and having to stretch international students’ fees to cover shortfalls in teaching home students and research) exist elsewhere, if not always to quite the same degree, in every other part of the UK too.

Moreover, one of the factors that has brought the funding problems to a head in Scotland are the UK-wide migration rules. The fall in international students prompted by changes to migration rules is, obviously, a particularly big problem when you are especially reliant on their fees.

So even though today’s report does not suggest specific solutions, which are left for another day, it should be read south of the border in England as well as in Wales and Northern Ireland just as much as it is pored over by policymakers in Edinburgh.

The side dish

Finally, the report is not primarily written for those, like many HEPI readers, who live and breathe higher education every day. For them, the story it reveals will already be familiar because, for example, they will already know about the sector’s funding shortfalls.

Nonetheless, elements of the report may still prove useful to the cognoscenti, and none more so than the list provided under ‘Regulatory and reporting burden’.

Running to six pages, this provides a top-level overview of the burdens on Scottish institutions (most of which will sound familiar elsewhere too). Each single point on the list makes perfect sense on its own of course, which is why regulatory bonfires are always so hard to achieve in practice, but together they add up to the most ridiculously costly and time-consuming burden imaginable. For the Higher Education Statistics Authority (HESA) alone, ’10 main returns are required each year, covering millions of data items for each institution.’

Given how many datapoints are collected from institutions, it is ironic that this report, which lays bare the true challenges facing Scottish institutions, rests only on a very limited set of the more heavily-used indicators (above all TRAC) rather than on all the other data that we collect and then, as this report shows, often tend to do next-to-nothing with. Some of that information may not be needed at all; some may not be entirely useless but may still come with an unacceptable opportunity cost.

I wonder if it might make sense to seek a quick win here while the rest of the Future Framework continues to roll the pitch for what could, in time, produce the most significant changes to higher education funding in Scotland for decades.

title: Public benefit with private investment: Lincoln Bishop University to become part of GUS
summary:
This guest blog has been kindly written for HEPI by Matt Innes, Senior Strategic Advisor and Executive Group Member of Lincoln Bishop University. Matt explains the rationale behind a big change for his institution. In the increasingly noisy policy debate about UK higher education, there is only one real point of consensus; that universities in […]

The post Public benefit with private investment: Lincoln Bishop University to become part of GUS appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This guest blog has been kindly written for HEPI by Matt Innes, Senior Strategic Advisor and Executive Group Member of Lincoln Bishop University. Matt explains the rationale behind a big change for his institution.

In the increasingly noisy policy debate about UK higher education, there is only one real point of consensus; that universities in the UK are operating in a financial environment that is structurally unsustainable.

While diagnosis of sector-wide financial distress focuses on a small number of related causes, the prescriptions for radical action in response are varied and often contradictory.

Some commentators advocate for a significant reduction in provider numbers, others call for government-led interventions, which – even if focused on institutions in distress – would potentially create levers to reshape and resize the sector. Ministers have meanwhile made it clear they will not introduce an ‘insolvency regime’ and that a sector which prizes institutional autonomy above almost everything else will need to find its own solutions.

Recent reports place a spotlight on the actions universities have taken in response to financial pressures and the potential impact on the quality of student experience and outcomes. The Office for Students’ recently published Business plan 2026-27 has signalled that, alongside institutional financial sustainability, it will have an increased focus on the impact of cost-saving measures on students.

But what of smaller higher education institutions facing financial pressures and where quality remains high? Universities where student satisfaction numbers are the envy of the sector and where the access agenda and civic mission are critical to the regional economy.

These smaller institutions often have a much more limited number of traditional levers, either to reduce costs or secure loans from increasingly risk-averse banks. So what options can they explore to protect the interests of student, staff and communities?

Challenging assumptions

Today, Lincoln Bishop University has provided its answer, confirming an agreement that will see the University become part of Global University Systems (GUS) – the global education group, subject to regulatory approvals.

This represents a significant moment for the sector. This is a new model; not a merger in the mould of the UCL Institute of Education, City St Georges or Kent and Greenwich. Lincoln Bishop University Ltd will function as an autonomous higher education institution, operating alongside a charitable foundation that will act as trustee of the institution’s founding endowments. There will be no changes to values, mission, teaching, student support or academic governance, and we will continue to be fully registered and regulated by the Office for Students, as at present.

Why is this model interesting? After all, the UK higher education sector already consists of a range of providers of varying character, size and shape, and since the Higher Education and Research Act (2017), all have operated on a ‘level playing field’ which allows diversity in corporate structure within a consistent framework set by the Office for Students’s Conditions of Registration.

Almost all UK universities already operate business models which combine access to the publicly-backed student loan book and limited direct public funding with commercialised funding streams from knowledge exchange, transnational education and international student recruitment. They rely on privately-owned service platforms in their core student recruitment and support activities, and increasingly adopt group structures which allow educational charities operating under Royal Charter to operate for-profit subsidiaries.

What is different here is that an established university, founded within the Church of England and rooted in public service and social purpose, is choosing to collaborate with a global group committed to long-term investment in higher education to deliver on its strategic objectives and ensure its longer-term financial sustainability.

In exploring a range of options, the University Executive and Council were determined to find a solution that protected Lincoln Bishop’s character, ethos and strategic vision and which preserved its commitment to widening access and responding to skills needs. The focus was on maintaining student choice and diversity of higher education provision, alongside protecting a critical element in the ecosystem for teacher training and professional development in early years and Special Educational Needs and Disabilities.

The model Lincoln Bishop is pursuing with Global University Systems opens up a route to preserve its significant regional impact, while allowing the University to reach out and scale up.

A position of strength

While Lincoln Bishop has faced financial challenges, it continues to perform strongly across a number of key metrics. UCAS and PGCE Applications are up by over 20% for 2026 entry, five times the sector average, and the University has ranked in the UK’s top five institutions for three consecutive years in the National Student Survey.

It also performs above sector norms in relation to the Office for Students’s Condition B3, with undergraduate first degree continuation 5% above threshold, completion 15% above threshold and progression 9% above threshold. This is a considerable achievement for a University with such high numbers of ‘first-in-family’ students, where three quarters of students are disadvantaged according to one or more Access & Participation Plan criteria, and where a third declare a disability. Those students go on to succeed: 18 months after graduation, 77% are in highly-skilled occupations and a further 17% in medium-skilled roles.

The University is critical to Lincolnshire, which has among the lowest rates of educational attainment in the country. It works with over 700 partner schools, training more than 1,000 future teachers at any one time, and has a distinctive civic footprint rooted in Social Purpose.

The motivation

This arrangement is not about quick wins. The University has been transparent that it will likely be 2028/29 before it returns to surplus, even with shareholder support. The attraction lies in long‑term value, mission alignment and the opportunity to support a high‑quality institution with a proud history and strong foundations.

The need to evolve

The Post-16 Education and Skills White Paper published last October, was clear in its direction of travel, wanting universities to ‘identify their specialism and foster collaboration with local market actors’, operating on the basis of differentiation and collaboration. It recognised that this would necessitate institutions becoming increasingly agile and innovative in exploring partnerships. That is precisely what Lincoln Bishop has done.

But the White Paper’s ambitions need a different regulatory approach. At present, individual institutions exploring innovative partnership propositions carry significant risk. They need a regulatory approach that is designed to support collaborations, partnerships, mergers or acquisitions within the framework of a regulated market.

Institutions such as Lincoln Bishop, with strong civic missions, are essential to regional skills pipelines, teacher training, healthcare provision and social mobility. Without new partnership models, many will face avoidable decline, with significant consequences for students, communities and local economies.

Together, Lincoln Bishop University and Global University Systems will combine private investment with public benefit, committed to excellence in teaching and research, quality and standards, and outstanding student outcomes.

If higher education is to remain diverse, mission‑driven and regionally anchored, partnerships such as this will be an important part of the sector’s future.

title: There’s nothing ‘Mickey Mouse’ about my Van Halen thesis | Letter
summary:
Asking specific questions about culture and answering them with care is what universities have been doing for a long time, writes Greg White

Reform UK’s disavowal of “Mickey Mouse degrees” (Report, 20 August) prompts me to disclose my own proposed thesis subject at the Suella Braverman Institute of Culture and Media Studies: “Do the Runaways, Cheap Trick, and Van Halen form three distinct subgenres in late 70s/early 80s rock music?”

Consider the rigorous training such a study would provide for modern working life. First, archival work in NME and Sounds, and distinguishing between primary sources (the records) and secondary sources (gig reviews from the periods in question).

full_text:
Reform UK’s disavowal of “Mickey Mouse degrees” (Report, 20 August) prompts me to disclose my own proposed thesis subject at the Suella Braverman Institute of Culture and Media Studies: “Do the Runaways, Cheap Trick, and Van Halen form three distinct subgenres in late 70s/early 80s rock music?”

Consider the rigorous training such a study would provide for modern working life. First, archival work in NME and Sounds, and distinguishing between primary sources (the records) and secondary sources (gig reviews from the periods in question).

Second, making a cogent argument. I would need to define terms precisely. Is Joan Jett’s proto-punk different in intent from Cheap Trick’s power-pop melodicism, and is that different again from Van Halen’s technical hard rock? That is taxonomy, debate and evidence-handling.

Third, transferable skills: close listening, contextualising art within economics and social change, handling contradictory testimony, and writing to a strict word count. Employers surely value graduates who can take a messy dataset and turn it into a clear thesis.

If we dismiss this as frivolous, we also dismiss the habit of asking specific questions about culture and answering them with care. That habit is what universities have been doing for an awfully long time.

So good luck to Suella Braverman and Richard Tice with reversing 2,500 years of human intellectual progress. I’m sure Aristotle would have had a strong opinion on Eddie Van Halen’s tapping technique.

Greg White

Totton, Hampshire

title: Tennessee Promise Boosts College Enrollment and Attainment, Data Shows
summary:
Tennessee Promise Boosts College Enrollment and Attainment, Data Shows
Susan H. Greenberg Fri, 08/28/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Susan H. Greenberg
full_text:
Tennessee Promise, the first statewide tuition-free community college program in the country, significantly boosted college enrollment and degree attainment at minimal cost to the state, according to a recent working paper from the National Bureau of Economic Research.

Looking at 2000–2023 Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System and 2000–2024 American Community Survey data, the researchers found that after the statewide introduction of the Tennessee Promise program in 2015, college enrollment among traditional-age high school graduates grew by 5.4 percentage points. The effects were even greater for nonwhite and rural students, the paper notes.

Among community colleges, the advent of free tuition correlated with “a statistically significant” 15 percent increase in associate degrees conferred and a 24 percent increase in the number of students who transferred to bachelor’s degree programs, the researchers found.

The paper also addressed concerns among Promise program critics who argue that offering free community college diverts to two-year colleges students who might otherwise pursue a bachelor’s degree. Researchers found that Promise-eligible students in Tennessee were roughly 2.7 percentage points more likely than their peers to earn a bachelor's degree by the time they turned 24; women were 4.1 percentage points more likely.

The Tennessee Promise program, which covers the remaining difference between a student’s grant aid and their college’s tuition and mandatory fees, cost less than $1,000 per student per year, the NBER paper noted.

“Taken together, the results indicate that a simple, last-dollar tuition guarantee tied to community colleges can expand access and increase two-year degree completion without evidence of harm to four-year attainment, and with marginally significant evidence of gains in bachelor’s degree completion, even when implemented at scale,” the paper’s authors conclude.

title: 2 Calif. Bills Could Let More Community Colleges Grant 4-Year Degrees
summary:
2 Calif. Bills Could Let More Community Colleges Grant 4-Year Degrees
Olivia.sanchez Fri, 08/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

College leaders disagree about whether the expansion is a good idea.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Two California bills that would expand community college bachelor’s degree offerings in the state have advanced through the Assembly and could be up for final votes before the session ends on Monday.

The California Community College system has been offering bachelor’s degrees within strict parameters for more than 10 years. The new proposals would increase the kinds of programs community colleges can offer, in some cases even if a nearby public four-year university already offers similar programs. AB 2694 would require that colleges meet certain performance standards in order to offer bachelor’s degrees, and SB 960 would cap the number of bachelor’s degrees a community college could grant at 15 percent of the total number of associate degrees granted.

Despite the success the bills have seen so far in the Legislature, the question of whether community colleges should offer bachelor’s degrees at all has divided higher education leaders in the state. And even if the bills do pass, it’s unclear whether California Gov. Gavin Newsom would sign them into law. In 2024 and 2025, Newsom vetoed bills that would have allowed community colleges to grant bachelor’s degrees in nursing.

The sponsor of AB 2694, Democratic Assemblymember David Alvarez, said in a statement that his bill would make higher education more accessible to more people and allow community colleges to better address workforce shortages.

“Our economy has changed, our workforce needs have changed and our students have changed. Many are working adults, parents, caregivers and first-generation students who are rooted in their communities and cannot relocate or commute long distances to earn a degree,” Alvarez said in a statement. “We have regions facing shortages of nurses, technicians or other skilled professionals. When existing programs are not meeting that need, our community colleges should be empowered to respond to those workforce needs. Transfer pathways will remain essential, and CSU and UC will always be the backbone of baccalaureate education in California.”

At least 24 states already have laws that permit some community college bachelor’s programs, according to the Community College Research Center based at Teachers College at Columbia University. Still, enrollment data from last spring shows that only about 2 percent of all community college students were enrolled in a bachelor’s degree program, according to the CCRC.

Thomas Brock, director of the CCRC, said that these arrangements are in the best interest of students and communities, and the more community colleges work with public four-year colleges, the better.

Although policies that allow community colleges to grant bachelor’s degrees often have bipartisan support among legislators, they have become a major point of contention between two- and four-year college leaders around the country.

A spokesperson for the California State University system declined to comment on the legislation.

Rowena M. Tomaneng, deputy chancellor of the California Community College system, said in an email that her office supports the expansion of high-quality, affordable education pathways that contribute to economic opportunity and social mobility for people across the state.

“As our state’s economy continues to evolve, students need flexible and affordable options that prepare them for in-demand careers and the future of work,” Tomaneng wrote.

Eloy Ortiz Oakley, who served as chancellor of the California Community College system from 2016 to 2022, disagreed. He said that community colleges would be better off creating workforce credentials or partnering with private nonprofit colleges to offer bachelor’s degrees than creating their own.

“Community colleges continue to twist themselves into pretzels trying to find an angle that allows them to offer more baccalaureate degrees, and I think that’s a mistake,” said Oakley, who is now president and CEO of the College Futures Foundation. “I think we’re missing the point in California.”

Oakley pointed to declining interest in traditional higher education and growing enthusiasm for shorter-term programs that are responsive to the evolving workforce as evidence that community colleges should put their energy elsewhere.

Jose L. Fierro, president and superintendent of Cerritos College in Southern California, agrees that community colleges should focus on regional workforce development and socioeconomic mobility for their students by offering associate degree and certificate programs. But, in some cases, they can also include bachelor’s degree programs, he said.

Cerritos began offering a bachelor’s of science in dental hygiene last fall. And starting in spring 2027, Cerritos will offer a bachelor’s degree in field ironworker supervision, which is meant to prepare students for leadership positions in the construction industry.

Fierro said he got pushback from leaders of California State University campuses that offer construction management when he proposed the program. They were concerned that Cerritos’s new program might enroll students who would have otherwise gone to their universities. Fierro said he expects very little overlap of interested students because Cerritos’s program is designed to serve primarily working adults who are already involved with local labor unions.

“It’s very unlikely that someone with a family, with a good-paying job, is going to quit their job and move 300 miles away to take a program and come back,” Fierro said.

Carlo Salerno, managing director of education insights at the Burning Glass Institute, a labor and policy think tank, said the community college bachelor’s degree debate is representative of a larger shift in higher education: the blurring of the traditional boundaries between two- and four-year colleges. For example, more four-year universities are offering professional certificates and other short-term opportunities for graduates to build on their education. He said he’s generally a proponent of the way higher education is evolving, but he understands why the changes are stressful to college leaders.

“There are only so many students out there that can be trained, and so I think both school structures are trying to make the case that, like, ‘Hey, look, if you want us to abide by our traditional roles, then let us abide by our traditional roles, but stay out of my student pool,’” Salerno said.

At the same time, he said, “Maybe we don’t have to adhere to two-year programs [providing] vocational training and four-year programs [offering] traditional bachelor’s degrees just because we’ve always done it that way.”

title: Turning High School Credentials Into College Credit
summary:
Turning High School Credentials Into College Credit
Joshua.Bay Fri, 08/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

Maine’s public universities will award up to eight credits for career-readiness microcredentials, giving students an early start toward a degree.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
Giving students college credit for career-readiness learning they’re already doing could achieve more than give them a head start on a degree. For students who may not see college as an option, Maine’s public universities are betting that having credits in hand could change whether they see a degree as within reach.

Starting this fall, the University of Maine System will award academic credit for microcredentials earned by high school students through Jobs for Maine’s Graduates, a statewide nonprofit that helps students transition into college or meaningful careers.

Through the agreement, announced Wednesday, students can earn up to eight college credits for JMG microcredentials that demonstrate mastery of such skills as financial and digital literacy, entrepreneurship, and leadership development.

The initiative is aimed especially at students who may not already see college as part of their future. JMG serves more than 13,000 students annually, and most enter the program without plans to attend college, according to the organization.

Kimberley Acker Lipp, chief executive officer of JMG, said nearly 70 percent of the students the organization serves come from economically disadvantaged households where neither parent attended college. For many of those students, she said, college can feel unfamiliar or out of reach.

“They don’t see themselves as college-going, and then underneath that, they don’t understand the different pathways that are available to them to get to college,” Lipp said. “This engenders confidence, and it also creates a new understanding and fluency of the postsecondary pathways that are available to them.”

The initiative: Under the new program, JMG students can earn the microcredentials as portable digital badges over multiple years of high school, with each Maine system institution determining how many college credits they are worth.

Craig Larrabee, chief executive officer of GenUS, a national affiliate of JMG, said the initiative reflects a broader shift away from thinking about postsecondary education exclusively in terms of four-year degree attainment and toward a wider range of credentials.

“Higher education is no longer just about degree attainment—it’s a credentialing world,” Larrabee said. “There are so many pathways and pipelines, if you will, of opportunities, yet we’re not having that conversation with high school students.”

The microcredentials could ultimately lead students toward a degree or provide a foundation for other credentials and career avenues, he added.

The agreement also marks the first time faculty governance groups at Maine’s public universities have agreed to accept microcredentials for college credit, according to the organization. The university system evaluated the JMG courses through the same process it uses to determine whether to award credit for prior learning, including work and military experience.

JMG collaborated with the Maine system on developing the microcredential framework early in the process, Lipp said, adapting an existing college-success program that supports students through age 24. How the credits apply will vary by institution.

“Some may count for elective credit, and some may count—for example, financial literacy may count as a personal financial literacy 101 course on other campuses,” Lipp said.

Why this matters: The partnership builds on JMG’s programming across all 16 Maine counties and its long-standing relationship with Maine’s public universities. Larrabee said recognizing learning students have already completed could be particularly valuable for those who have historically confronted obstacles to higher education.

“Those students that are facing educational barriers, those students that do not have the currency, if you will, of other students, their backgrounds lean them towards possibly making poor decisions,” Larrabee said. “Recognizing and validating durable skills is creating a level of confidence for these young people.”

The new program comes as Maine looks to increase the share of residents with postsecondary credentials. The state has set a goal for 70 percent of working-age adults to hold a credential that leads to a good job by 2035. Today, about 55 percent of Maine residents hold such a credential, a gap Lipp said the new program could help narrow.

“Many students can benefit,” Lipp said. “They’re leaving high school with eight college credits that they’ve earned by attaining these credentials. That gives them something very valuable to take with them.”

The approach could eventually extend beyond Maine. Education systems in Kansas, Kentucky, West Virginia and Wisconsin are considering similar models, according to JMG.

“Students develop and mature at different rates as they’re leaving high school, and there’s a lot of students who, while they’re in high school, don’t succeed in traditional academics,” Lipp said. “Allowing students to be celebrated and recognized for attaining durable skills is another way to give them the confidence that they can pursue postsecondary education.”

title: The Ivies Brought Back Test Scores, but 90% of Colleges Still Don’t Require Them
summary:
The Ivies Brought Back Test Scores, but 90% of Colleges Still Don’t Require Them
Johanna Alonso Fri, 08/28/2026 - 03:00 AM

New data from FairTest shows that standardized tests are a condition of admission at just a few colleges, and even among the highest-ranked universities, the majority remain test optional for this academic year.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
In the six years since most colleges and universities suspended admissions testing requirements amid the COVID-19 pandemic, many have reinstated the requirement or announced plans to do so, including all of the Ivy League universities. But data collected by FairTest, an organization that advocates against the use of tests in admissions, shows that the requirements have not, in fact, had a major resurgence.

In the organization’s analysis of 2,247 admissions policies for the 2026–27 admissions cycle, only 7 percent—or 161 colleges—require test scores for admission. The vast majority, 86 percent, are test optional—students may submit scores if they so choose—while 4 percent are test free, meaning they will not look at test scores. Only 11 institutions introduced new testing requirements for this admission cycle, but another 10 switched from test required to test optional this year. The total number of colleges requiring test scores increased by just one.

Those numbers shift only slightly when looking at top-ranked institutions. Among top institutions—any university that U.S. News & World Report has included in its top 100 ranking—11 percent require scores, versus 82 percent that are test optional. Two Ivy League institutions, Columbia University and Princeton University, remain test optional for this admissions cycle but will switch to requiring scores next year; two other Ivy-Plus institutions, Duke University and the University of Chicago, are remaining test optional indefinitely.

The data, which FairTest releases annually, comes amid widespread debate over whether more colleges should reintroduce these requirements. Some faculty members in the University of California system have argued in favor of the requirements, saying that a significant portion of their students are not cut out for college coursework and considering SAT or ACT scores in admissions could weed out unprepared students. And with all eight Ivy League institutions reinstating the requirements, some higher education experts question whether other selective institutions plan to follow suit.

The Trump administration has also placed a heavy emphasis on the use of tests in admissions. The administration’s higher education compact, an agreement the government asked institutions to sign in exchange for preferential treatment in research funding last October, would have required institutions to make admissions decisions based on “objective criteria” and mandate all applicants to submit scores. Recent Department of Justice investigations into alleged discrimination against white and Asian students in medical and law school admissions have centered around disparities in MCAT and LSAT scores by race.

But Harry Feder, FairTest’s executive director, said the discourse around test requirements distracts from the fact that the vast majority of schools are continuing with test-optional admissions.

“The narrative that is being put forward … says, ‘Oh, the world is going back to testing.’ But it’s just not true, and it’s a story that is essentially being driven by what the Ivy Plus are doing or have done, which is going back to testing for their own reasons,” said Feder.

Advocates for the use of test scores in admissions argue that the tests are better predictors of college academic performance than high school GPA and that grade inflation in high schools makes the scores even more valuable. But critics cite recent research showing that GPA is a much better predictor at public colleges. Other research shows massive disparities in how students perform on the SAT based on race and familial income, in part because wealthier students can afford test-preparation materials and tutoring that others cannot.

The debate also embroils public institutions that have tightened their testing policies. The university systems in Florida and Tennessee are the only public systems that require standardized test scores at every campus. But the University System of Georgia increased the number of institutions where scores are required from three to seven for this admissions cycle; for consideration at some of the remaining 19 colleges, students must submit test scores if their grade point average falls below a certain threshold.

Three other flagship universities—Ohio State University, Purdue University, and the University of Texas at Austin—also require scores. But generally, public institutions require tests slightly less frequently than colleges over all (6 percent).

Among private colleges, it’s not just highly selective institutions that require test scores; of the institutions that require SAT scores, about half are religiously affiliated institutions and about 30 are seminaries, rabbinical schools, yeshivas or Bible colleges.

Lisa Carlton, president of the Independent Educational Consultants Association, which represents independent college counselors, said that, even though 90 percent of colleges do not require test scores, most counselors encourage students to take the tests anyway. Test-optional colleges all consider test scores differently, and some admit very few students who don’t submit scores despite not requiring them. In the 2025–26 application cycle, the portion of applicants who sent in test scores (51 percent) surpassed those who did not for the first time since 2020, according to Common App data.

“What we’re seeing is, because of grade inflation, it’s very hard for the colleges to get a full academic read and some of them really want to see that score as a validator, if you will,” she said. “But on the other hand, there are schools that are genuinely test optional and have found a way to evaluate candidates without test scores.”

title: Minister promises review as schools criticise DEIS Plus process
summary: Several principals of schools omitted from the DEIS Plus scheme told Prime Time they believe the process didn't fully capture the true scale of need in their area
full_text:
Minister for Education Hildegarde Naughton has said a new multimillion-euro funding scheme for disadvantaged urban schools will be "reviewed and monitored" after principals of schools excluded from the initiative raised concerns around the fairness of the process used to access which schools qualify for inclusion.

Some 129 schools have been included in the DEIS Plus programme which provides a range of additional supports including a full-time teacher dedicated to promoting mental health and wellbeing.

Minister Naughton told RTÉ's Prime Time that she was "not happy in relation to the level of data" available to her department and said she had asked officials to work with other government agencies, including the Department of Justice, to improve the information used to assess schools.

However, she stressed the criteria has to be comparable across schools.

Several principals of schools omitted from the scheme told Prime Time they believe the process didn't fully capture the true scale of need in their area.

Among them is Aine Carthy, of St Paul’s National School in Drogheda.

Standing in the schoolyard speaking to Prime Time, she pointed at two houses at either end of the campus. One is where remains of 17 year-old Keane Mulready-Woods, a former student of the school, were discovered, the other excavated as part of the search for missing child, Kyran Durnin.

"Our children have to walk by those premises on their way to school every day. They know that children in their world can be murdered. If that doesn’t count towards being a disadvantaged community, I don't know what does," Ms Carthy said.

The principal, who has taught at St Paul’s for 18 years, was "devastated" to learn it had not been included in the DEIS Plus scheme. Ms Carthy outlined how in the school’s 44-year history 80 past pupils have died, many from drugs, suicide and murder.

"There's so much trauma in the community. Our children are living with grieving parents, grieving grandparents, on top of the impact of drugs. It’s heartbreaking."

While Drogheda, the country’s largest town, will have no DEIS Plus schools, there are now seven in Dundalk.

"If they were transparent in what the criteria were, there's nothing that we would not meet or surpass when compared to schools that have been given DEIS Plus," Ms Carthy added.

"We genuinely thought it was a mistake. I emailed the minister saying, 'I assume there’s been an error’?"'

St Paul's serves a community which includes areas designated ‘extremely disadvantaged’ in the Pobal Deprivation Index, one of a number of indicators the Department says it has used to calculate eligibility.

A separate DEIS Plus Index was also developed as part of the assessment process. This new index includes greater weighting for unemployment and lone parenthood.

Children from Roma and Traveller backgrounds along with those living in State emergency accommodation such as IPAS are also priority indicators, according to the Department of Education.

But Aine Carthy maintains parents often don’t tell a school about their ethnic background and that a paper-based exercise can’t fully capture a picture of disadvantage within the school.

Some 123 schools appealed their exclusion from the scheme but just eight were successful.

The Department of Education has acknowledged "complex local pressures" can’t be fully captured in its methodologies and said it was looking at ways to improve it in the future.

"I will be ensuring that my department is getting access to even more granular data so that we're getting the best information," Minister Naughton said.

St Michael’s Infant School in Limerick City is another school that was unsuccessful in its appeal to be included in the DEIS Plus Scheme.

"I'm not afraid to say I cried the day we found out. I was genuinely devastated," Principal Tracie Tobin told Prime Time.

Unlike some other educational funding processes there was no opportunity to provide local context or nuance about her school community, she suggested. Schools have also not been given a score to determine how close they were to inclusion.

"How do they know what's going on in families from a PPS number or from an address? I know the department has to have a framework but it’s very clinical, the contextual piece is missing."

"As a teacher, the most important trait that you have is to be fair when it comes to children. We understand fairness, and do I think this is a fair process? No."

Questions have also been raised by academics about the transparency of the selection methodology.

Assistant professor at Trinity College, Barra Roantree, previously undertook socioeconomic research in Dublin's south west inner city. He was surprised to see that many of the existing DEIS schools in the area were not included in the new scheme.

"The area has pockets of deprivation that are as bad as anywhere else in the inner city, and less than half the schools that are already in the DEIS programme got DEIS Plus," he told the programme.

Other parts of Dublin have also received low allocations of DEIS Plus, while in contrast, all the DEIS primary schools in the north east inner city were included in the scheme, Dr Roantree said.

"We don't know fully what goes into the department’s new index. The exact details that would be needed to replicate it, haven’t been published.

"We've just been told to essentially take it for granted that the statistical methodology used is adequate."

Speaking on Prime Time, Minister Naughton said she has asked her department to publish more details of the selection methodology.

"Once published, the methodology will be fully transparent and replicable. The factors used to construct the index will be clearly defined and based on Census data," a statement from the department added.

It said schools would be able to calculate their "average deprivation" score but not recreate their specific Deis score as it is a "relative measure calculated in the context of the demographic profiles and scores of all schools."

Minister Naughton defended the use of a standardised model to determine which schools receive additional supports.

"We have to have a model that I can apply to the 4,000 schools across the country, because one school's perspective in relation to disadvantage may be very different to another," she said.

129 schools have been included in the current Deis Plus designation - 102 primary and 27 post-primary schools. €16 million is being spent this year, rising to €48 million in 2027 to introduce the new scheme and support the wider 10-year Deis strategy.

title: Vik Singh, Austrade
summary:
This week, The PIE sat down with Vik Singh, trade and investment commissioner for Austrade in South Asia, to discuss Australian education’s expanding footprint in India, how closer industry links could create better pathways into work for students, and how he is getting on with his Spanish-learning streak.

The post Vik Singh, Austrade appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Describe yourself in three words or phrases.

Committed, innovative and loyal.

What do you like most about your job?

I love that I get to meet people from all facets of international and domestic education across the region. I also love being able to support more Australian universities, institutions and edtech companies as they enter India and South Asia, and help a business or university be successful.

Describe a project or initiative you’re currently working on that excites you.

If we can solve the problem — or create an opportunity — for all students studying with or in Australia to have almost guaranteed employment pathways, while giving companies access to a new talent pipeline and the ability to inform future course direction, that would be amazing.

What’s a piece of work you’re proud of – and what did it teach you?

There are a number of things from the past few years that I’m exceptionally proud of, but one is seeing how deeply Australian education is now embedded in India. It taught me humility and the power of perseverance — and that good things come to those who work hard.

What’s a small daily habit that helps you in your work?

It’s not so much a daily habit for work, but I switch off my mind by playing Duolingo. I’m learning Spanish at the moment and have kept up the streak for 490 days!

What’s one change you’d like to see in your sector over the next few years?

I’d like to see more equity and access to education across India and South Asia. I’d love to see more underprivileged children able to access the quality of education we are seeing around us here. That is probably my number one priority.

What’s one piece of advice you’d give to someone starting out in this field?

Keep the student at the centre of everything you do. If you approach every decision through the lens of what is best for the student, you can never go wrong.

title: Minerva Project launches global university system to scale HE model
summary:
Minerva Project has announced plans to establish a global network of universities based on the educational model developed for its flagship Minerva University, with governments, philanthropists and existing institutions invited to establish new member universities.

The post Minerva Project launches global university system to scale HE model appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The San Francisco-based education company said the new Minerva University System will let new institutions operate under the Minerva name and use its curriculum designs, faculty model, assessment framework and Forum learning platform.

The institutions will be structured similarly to members of a public university system, with each university designed around the needs of its country, student population or academic discipline.

“No country has ever been able to tell its people, ‘We are building you a Harvard,’” said Ben Nelson, founder and CEO of Minerva Project.

“That is what we are offering. Not a franchise of an American university, and not a campus that exports a diluted version of traditional curriculum, but a Minerva University built for that country, that student population, or that interdisciplinary domain.”

Speaking exclusively to The PIE News, Nelson said that he anticipated interest for the project on a global scale. “Obviously, we are based in the United States – and we believe that there is enormous need in the United States for more models of higher education to demonstrate what’s possible – but at the same time, we’ve seen demand for Minerva programs and Minerva institutions all over the world,” he explained.

He pointed out that Minerva has “a large number of engagements” in Latin America., as well as significant demand in East and Central Asia.

Minerva Project was founded in 2011 with the aim of redesigning higher education “from first principles”. Its first institution, Minerva University, opened in 2014 with 25 students and received independent accreditation from the WASC Senior College and University Commission in 2021.

Since 2021, the organisation has also worked with partner institutions to implement elements of its model. It said it has trained more than 1,000 instructors and reached more than 50,000 learners at institutions across the US, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and the Americas.

The model combines cognitive and behavioural science with problem- and project-based learning and a defined set of measurable capabilities, which are taught through active and applied learning methods.

We’ve seen demand for Minerva programs and Minerva institutions all over the world

Ben Nelson, Minerva Project

Minerva said its expansion through a university system is partly driven by the need to equip students with skills that will remain valuable as artificial intelligence develops.

“AІ literacy modules and policy statements are not enough to ensure humans retain their agency and value in the face of artificial superintelligence,” the organisation said.

Nelson said the system would seek to accelerate the development of what he calls “critical wisdom” – the ability to think critically and systematically and apply those skills to new challenges and contexts.

“We need to reach hundreds of millions of students, not thousands,” he said. “We have a tested solution, and we are bringing it to the world.”

Minerva is now preparing to issue a formal call for founders and said it is already in discussions with four groups interested in establishing member institutions.

These include governments seeking to develop workforce and leadership capacity; philanthropists and benefactors looking to establish new universities; owners of dormant or newly licensed institutions with accreditation; and established universities looking to expand their portfolios and introduce new programs under the Minerva banner.

Nelson told The PIE that some of these partnerships are already in the works. “We’ve been working on this concept for a number of months and have engaged in conversations with a number of prospective groups and even existing institutions that have said, ‘Hey, could we launch an entire Minerva University?'” he said.

Founders will work with Minerva Project to establish each institution’s vision, academic focus, student model and location.

Member universities will share infrastructure, follow Minerva’s academic standards and participate in ongoing innovation and improvement, according to the organisation.

title: Creating pathways to Associate Professor (Learning and Teaching)
summary: The post Creating pathways to Associate Professor (Learning and Teaching) appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Dr Stacie Gray, Academic Practice Lead at the University of Northampton, shares lessons learned from designing an Associate Professor (Learning and Teaching) development programme.

The journey towards Associate Professor (Learning and Teaching) begins long before colleagues consider applying for progression. Creating space to explore educational leadership earlier in their careers can help colleagues:

recognise the breadth of educational leadership that supports progression

understand how different experiences connect

make meaningful choices about their future development.

These insights emerged through the design of a development programme for aspiring associate professors (Learning and Teaching) at the University of Northampton (UON). Through designing this programme, I identified three key considerations that may be valuable for institutions seeking to develop similar pathways:

Supporting holistic educational leadership development.

Creating opportunities for structured reflection.

Ensuring representation of diverse leadership journeys.

Holistic educational leadership development

One of the key considerations during the design process was how to support colleagues to explore the breadth of educational leadership. While dedicated sessions can enable deeper exploration of broad practice areas, participants are encouraged to draw connections between areas, recognise where their existing expertise contributes across multiple dimensions of educational leadership and identify opportunities for future growth.

Using the Professional Standards Framework (PSF) as a developmental framework was particularly helpful. Mapping sessions to relevant PSF dimensions helped create a well-rounded developmental pathway, ensuring broad coverage of educational leadership while reinforcing opportunities for reflection throughout the programme.

Structured reflection

Embedded within sessions throughout the programme and supported through a reflective journal assessment, reflection is positioned as an ongoing process of sense-making that enables colleagues to:

identify strengths, areas for growth and future opportunities

consider the breadth of their educational leadership contribution

connect experiences as they emerge and understand how they contribute to their development

build their leadership narrative over time, rather than trying to reconstruct a leadership narrative when progression becomes an immediate consideration.

I developed a set of prompts to help colleagues articulate and evidence their contribution to learning and teaching, while simultaneously supporting their attainment of Senior Fellowship through UON’s Advance HE Accredited Academic and Professional Practice Scheme.

The reflective prompts could be adopted by institutions developing similar educational leadership pathways or incorporated into Senior Fellowship development activities.

Representation

By showcasing the diversity of educational leadership across learning and teaching, the programme aims to:

broaden understanding of diverse educational leadership journeys and practice

remain accessible to colleagues from different professional contexts and background

encourage participants to reflect on how cross-disciplinary and cross-professional relationships might expand their networks, and influence opportunities for their future development.

My recent transition from an academic role within a faculty to a professional services role as Academic Practice Lead reinforced this thinking. Experiencing both contexts highlighted the diverse ways colleagues contribute to learning and teaching, with some of the most significant contributions emerging through collaboration across academic and professional services teams.

The value of a dedicated development programme

My motivation for developing the programme stemmed from my own journey towards Associate Professor (Learning and Teaching). While the destination was clear, I found myself navigating several questions along the way. How do different dimensions of educational leadership come together in practice? What does educational leadership look like beyond my immediate context? How do I access and engage with the wider areas of educational leadership that sit beyond my own experience and networks?

These reflections inspired a dedicated development programme for UON colleagues that enables them to:

explore educational leadership more holistically and intentionally at an earlier point in their career

recognise and capture their leadership contributions as they emerge

reflect on strengths and opportunities for further development

build a meaningful, personalised pathway for their progression.

How is your institution creating earlier developmental opportunities for colleagues to holistically reflect on, and meaningfully grow, their educational leadership over time?

title: Nicht-staatliche Hochschulen haben spezifische Transferprofile
summary: Im Rahmen des vom BMFTR geförderten Forschungsprojektes nsh-inno untersuchte das CHE in Kooperation mit dem Fraunhofer ISI die Transfer-Beiträge von Hochschulen in...
full_text:
Im Rahmen des vom BMFTR geförderten Forschungsprojektes nsh-inno untersuchte das CHE in Kooperation mit dem Fraunhofer ISI die Transfer-Beiträge von Hochschulen in privater und kirchlicher Trägerschaft. Zum Abschluss des Projektes veröffentlichen das CHE und das Fraunhofer ISI drei Fallstudien, die illustrieren, dass die Transfer-Aktivitäten und -Zielgruppen privater und kirchlicher Hochschulen sich je nach fachlichem und regionalem Kontext unterscheiden.

Die Bucerius Law School ist eine rein auf Rechtswissenschaften spezialisierte Universität in Hamburg. Trägerin der Hochschule ist die ZEIT STIFTUNG BUCERIUS, die sich als „Förderin und Teil einer liberalen, offenen Zivilgesellschaft“ versteht. Dieses Ziel wird von der Hochschule zum einen durch die Ausbildung von hoch qualifizierten Jurist*innen und zum anderen durch die Förderung von und das Engagement in gesellschaftlichen Debatten und Gesetzgebungsverfahren verfolgt.

Die breite Öffentlichkeit informiert die Hochschule über öffentliche Veranstaltungen, YouTube-Videos oder auch durch mediale Beiträge über gesellschaftspolitische und juristische Themen. Multiplikatoren wie z. B. Politik, Verbände oder Vertreter*innen von Professionen wie Soziale Arbeit, die mit Recht zu tun haben, werden mit Fachvorträgen/Fachartikeln, expliziten Stakeholder-Formaten wie Workshops, Hintergrundgesprächen und Weiterbildungsangeboten adressiert. Darüber hinaus wird von den Hochschulmitgliedern spezifische Expertise in konkrete Gesetzgebungs- oder Auslegungsprozesse eingebracht. Dies geschieht beispielsweise durch Artikel in Juristischen Fachzeitschriften, der Beteiligung an parlamentarischen Arbeitskreisen, durch Gesetzesvorschläge oder die Mitwirkung in Gesetzgebungsverfahren.

Die Katholische Hochschule für Sozialwesen Berlin (KHSB) fokussiert sich auf anwendungsorientierte Fragestellungen in den Bereichen Soziale Arbeit, Gesundheit, Erziehung und Bildung. Transfer wird von der Hochschule nicht als nachgelagerte Verwertung von Wissen verstanden, sondern als wechselseitiger, partizipativer und gesellschaftlich verantworteter Austausch zwischen Hochschule, Praxis, Politik und Zivilgesellschaft.

Ihre wichtigsten Transferpartner sind kommunale Verwaltungen, Wohlfahrtsverbände, kirchliche und freie Träger, gemeinnützige Organisationen oder Berufs- und Fachverbände. Eine besondere Rolle spielen aber inzwischen auch Bürger*innen, Nachbarschaften und Nutzer*innen sozialer Dienstleistungen.

Die Transfermechanismen sind vielfältig. So werden partizipative Forschungsprojekte, Forschungskooperationen mit zivilgesellschaftlichen Akteuren sowie ko-kreative Formate mit Praxispartnern durchgeführt. Wissen wird aber auch im Rahmen von Praxis- und Politikberatung, Fachtagungen, Fachkonsultationen, wissenschaftlicher Weiterbildung und dem Engagement von Lehrenden in Gremien und Verbänden vermittelt. Hinzu kommen Formen des Personaltransfers, etwa über Praktika, studentische Projekte, Abschlussarbeiten, Community Service und den dualen Studiengang.

Die Alanus Hochschule in Alfter bei Bonn ist die größte private Kunsthochschule Deutschlands, die aber zugleich auch gesellschaftswissenschaftliche Fachbereiche hat. Entsprechend nennt sie sich „Hochschule für Kunst und Gesellschaft“ und hat den Anspruch, künstlerische und wissenschaftliche Arbeit in gesellschaftliche Kontexte hineinzutragen und aktiv zu gesellschaftlichen Entwicklungs- und Transformationsprozessen beizutragen.

Das Transferprofil der Alanus Hochschule ist durch ein breites und heterogenes Spektrum an Transferpartnern gekennzeichnet. Im Fachbereich Wirtschaft kooperiert die Hochschule eng mit regionalen kleinen und mittleren Unternehmen, vor allem aus dem Nachhaltigkeits-, Bio- und anthroposophisch geprägten Umfeld. Ebenso wichtig sind jedoch Partner aus Bildung, Sozialwesen, Kultur und Zivilgesellschaft. In den künstlerischen, architektonischen und gesellschaftsbezogenen Fachbereichen spielen darüber hinaus Museen, Stiftungen, soziale Organisationen, Bürgerinitiativen und lokale Entwicklungsakteure eine wichtige Rolle.

Die Mechanismen des Wissenstransfers sind an der Alanus Hochschule besonders eng mit der Lehre verknüpft. Transfer erfolgt vor allem über studienintegrierte, projektförmige und praxisnahe Formate. Charakteristisch sind Lehrveranstaltungen, in denen Studierende gemeinsam mit externen Partnern an realen Problemstellungen arbeiten und konkrete Lösungen, Konzepte oder Gestaltungen entwickeln.

„Die drei Fallstudien zeigen, dass die Gruppe der nicht-staatlichen Hochschulen durch eine große Heterogenität gekennzeichnet ist und es nicht die typische private oder kirchliche Hochschule gibt“, erläutert Isabel Roessler, Projektverantwortliche seitens des CHE. „Unter den rund 150 Einrichtungen reicht das Spektrum von sehr kleinen, regional orientierten und fachlich spezialisierten Hochschulen bis hin zu großen Hochschulverbünden mit einer zweistelligen Anzahl von Standorten. Viele Standorte finden sich in größeren Städten und Ballungsgebieten, andere sind bewusst an eher kleineren bis sehr kleinen Orten gegründet worden“ so Roessler weiter.
